query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A high-throughput, containerless electromagnetic levitation platform integrated with real-time high-speed imaging and spectroradiometry, together with machine-learning enhanced ab initio simulation models, can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change on melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast high-entropy alloys produced by standard melting processes, representing a diverse compositional subset of single-phase HEAs with melting temperatures below ~2500 K.
generation.intervention: Utilize an automated electromagnetic levitation apparatus that heats the sample in a containerless, inert atmosphere while simultaneously capturing high-speed optical images and radiometric data. The experimental data are then fused with machine-learning surrogate models trained on ab initio molecular dynamics and calibrated against simpler binary/ternary systems.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed under containerless conditions to minimize heterogeneous nucleation and contamination; inert atmosphere; heating rates and temperature measurement resolution high enough to capture rapid phase transitions (microsecond resolution); applicability up to ~2500 K and for alloys with modest oxide content.
generation.structural_mediator: The establishment of a clean, homogeneous liquid-phase interface during melting, where precise optical and radiative signals directly reflect the microstructural evolution (melting onset, latent heat release, and volume change) that is subsequently interpreted by the machine-learning model.
generation.mechanism: Containerless processing minimizes extrinsic disturbances (e.g., nucleation on container walls), while high-speed, multi-signal acquisition captures the fast kinetics of melting. Machine-learning models, calibrated on well-characterized binary and ternary systems, interpolate and extrapolate these thermal signatures to extract latent heats (enthalpy and entropy of fusion) and melting-point shifts in complex HEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Accurate determination of melting temperature and fusion thermodynamics with errors below ±5% relative to conventional DSC benchmarks, along with reliable volume-change measurements. This represents an efficiency and precision improvement over traditional contact-based calorimetry, which typically has 10–15% uncertainty.
generation.baseline: Standard calorimetric methods (e.g., DSC in container-based systems) that are slower and subject to contamination and nucleation artifacts, leading to larger uncertainties (≈10–15%) and limited efficiency when screening across a wide compositional space.
generation.boundary: The method is expected to be applicable primarily to HEAs with melting temperatures up to ~2500 K and limited oxide or impurity levels. Its performance for alloys undergoing multiple, overlapping phase transformations or for systems with extreme chemical complexity beyond the calibrated machine-learning domain remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how well the machine-learning surrogate models, primarily trained on simpler binary/ternary systems, will generalize to the full compositional space of high-entropy alloys, especially in cases with subtle multi-phase transitions or atypical liquid structures.

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the proposed high-throughput containerless levitation approach to a benchmark HEA (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) with well-documented melting properties. Simultaneously, perform traditional DSC measurements for comparison.
measurements: Melting temperature determined via spectroradiometric analysis
Fusion enthalpy and entropy determined by integrating the calorimetric signal during melting
Volume change measured by high-speed imaging analysis correlated with density changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any of the measured quantities (melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, or volume change) differ from established benchmark values by more than ±5% (relative to DSC and literature data), then the hypothesis is rejected.
